clue.text: Runs down with £1,000 for sporting coups

blocks.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds
to run down someone is to criticise them harshly, to slam them

explanation.surface: A gambler or sports fan is criticised for taking a thousand pounds in exchange for winning bets on big sporting upsets.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the two halves in reverse order: the criticism comes first in the clue but second in the answer. 'Grand' for a thousand pounds is everyday British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis and golf, winning all four major championships in one year is the supreme achievement, a sporting triumph of the rarest kind.

clue.text: English insult offered up for French dramatist

indicators.note: in a down clue, something offered up is raised, so the letters read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
a dig is a snide remark or insult

explanation.surface: Someone is insulted in English as a way of getting at a French playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: E and DIG are joined first, then the whole run is read upwards to give GIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: André Gide was a French writer and Nobel laureate who wrote plays as well as novels and journals.

clue.text: Part of church where mobile phone use might be heard

indicators.note: something heard is taken by its sound, not its spelling

blocks.note: apps are the programs people use on their mobile phones

explanation.surface: A vicar worries that phones might ring out during a service in some part of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests ringtones echoing round a church; in fact the phone 'use' is apps, which sounds the same as the church part.
explanation.definitionFit: The apse is the semicircular, vaulted recess at the east end of a church, usually holding the altar.

clue.text: Express to voice anger

blocks.note: first meaning: to show or make clear a feeling or idea
second meaning: to protest publicly in a march or rally

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Express' look like the British newspaper, inviting a reading about a tabloid's outrage; it is simply the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both showing a feeling openly and taking part in a public protest march against something.

clue.text: Student deserved to become erudite

blocks.note: L for learner, as on a British learner driver's plate
to have earned something is to have deserved it

explanation.surface: A hard-working student earned the right to be considered a scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: Note the two-syllable pronunciation of the answer here, as in a learned professor.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone with deep scholarly knowledge gained by long study; they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Everyman receiving a knighthood – subsequently assuming initially dirty deals

indicators.note: whoever is receiving something takes it in, so one piece goes inside another
to assume is to take on or put on, so one piece takes another inside it
initially points to the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself, so Everyman is ME
taken as written
K is the abbreviation for a knighthood, as in KBE
so can mean then, afterwards
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: The setter, newly knighted, is suspected of shady dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: ME takes in A and K to make MAKE; SO takes in D to make SDO. 'Dirty deals' looks like a phrase, but 'deals' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To make do is to cope or manage with what is available, which is one sense of the verb to deal.

clue.text: Stradivari's taking in opera singer

indicators.note: what one word is taking in sits inside it, so the answer lies within the letters

blocks.note: the answer is concealed inside the violin maker's name

explanation.surface: A Stradivarius violin is accompanying a soprano at the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Stradivari was the famous Italian violin maker, which fits the musical picture neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: A diva is a celebrated female opera singer, a prima donna, the leading lady of the stage.

clue.text: Fail-safe if I do troop manœuvres

indicators.note: manoeuvres are movements and repositionings, so the letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An officer promises the plan cannot go wrong if he leads the troops on manoeuvres himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manœuvres' looks like a noun about army exercises, matching the troops, but it works as the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something designed so that even the most careless user cannot break or misuse it is built to never go wrong.

clue.text: Models cunning, getting fancy cars

blocks.note: arch means knowing or sly
the Jaguar E-Type is a classic, glamorous sports car

explanation.surface: Sly fashion models get themselves expensive sports cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an anagram signal for 'cars', but the four letters can't make enough; it is literal, describing the Jaguar sports cars.
explanation.definitionFit: An archetype is the original pattern or perfect typical example on which others are based, so a template or exemplar.

clue.text: Disturbed bird makes a little sound, heads off

indicators.note: something disturbed has been knocked out of its proper arrangement
a little of a word is just a small part of it, its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written
just the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A startled bird lets out a small noise and flies away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes' looks like the verb joining the parts, but it is part of the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Passengers who get off a ship or plane leave it and go on their way, so they depart from the vessel.

clue.text: In retrospect, I had doubts, ultimately, about record

indicators.note: retrospect means looking back, so the letters are read backwards
ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: I'd is the contraction of I had
the final letter of the word
C is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: Looking back, someone had misgivings about a recording they made.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the contraction I'D is turned round; the S and C follow on unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: A gramophone or vinyl record is a flat round platter, and the shape gives it its common name.

clue.text: Ready to meet Nelson at sea

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and lost, so these letters are in disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor stands prepared to greet Admiral Nelson aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the naval picture of Nelson perfectly, which hides its job as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone primed and determined to perform at their very best when tested, fully prepared.

clue.text: Source of wine from ancient river?

blocks.note: elder means older
a river is something that flows, so a flower in crossword terms

explanation.surface: A wine is said to come from some old, historic river valley.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords a river can be a 'flower' (rhyming with lower), since it flows; the question mark flags that trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The blossoms of the elder tree are used in Britain to make homemade wine and cordial, so they are what it is made from.

clue.text: Strong drink when harmonicas playing

indicators.note: instruments playing are making music, a lively scrambling of their sound into new patterns

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boozy tune strikes up in a bar where mouth organs are being played.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong drink' might suggest a spirit such as brandy, but the ten letters of the instrument rearrange into a cherry liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: Maraschino is a clear, sweet Italian liqueur distilled from marasca cherries, a potent alcoholic spirit.

clue.text: For whom 'proper bash' moves around?

indicators.note: something that moves around changes position, so its letters are relocated

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Some people's idea of a real night out is a party that keeps changing venue.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: those who move from pub to pub make the party travel with them.
explanation.definitionFit: People who visit one drinking place after another in an evening carry their celebration around town with them.

clue.text: Nowadays, timely journalist moved with the times

blocks.note: AD, anno Domini, marks the present era
apt means fitting or well-timed
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A reporter writing topical pieces these days has kept pace with modern trends.
explanation.walkthrough: AD as the current era stands in for 'nowadays'; editor is the usual crossword journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Changing your ways to suit new conditions is to adjust or modernise, keeping pace with change.

clue.text: Disciplined hospital employee

blocks.note: first meaning: neat, well-behaved and controlled
second meaning: an attendant doing non-medical work on a ward

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it looks like a description of a well-behaved hospital worker; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for tidy, regimented behaviour and a noun for a hospital attendant who carries and cleans.

clue.text: Really, a tango with Queen?

blocks.note: taken as written
tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet
one queen in a pack of cards is a heart, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: Someone asks in disbelief whether they will actually be dancing a tango with the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' wants to be ER or R; here it is a heart, by example, as the Queen of Hearts is a playing card, and the question mark signals the loose link.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in one's true nature or basically, the deep reality underneath outward appearances.

clue.text: Had made alterations to e.g. jeans

blocks.note: first meaning: fooled or deceived, as in 'you've been had'
second meaning: narrowed a garment at the seams to fit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Had made' reads as a past perfect verb, but the clue splits after 'Had', which means deceived.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both fooled by a trick and a garment narrowed by a tailor so it fits more tightly.

clue.text: Snarling crabby reclusive ornery old grouse (economical, primarily!)

definitions.text: Snarling crabby reclusive ornery old grouse (economical, primarily!)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is used

blocks.clueFragment: Snarling crabby reclusive ornery old grouse (economical
blocks.note: the first letters of these seven words

explanation.surface: A thumbnail sketch of a bad-tempered, stingy old miser.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is both a source letter and part of the description: the whole clue paints Dickens's miser.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer is Dickens's miserly, bad-tempered character in A Christmas Carol, now a byword for any skinflint.

clue.text: Extremely tense and hot before end of story

blocks.note: so means very or extremely
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
H for hot, as on a tap
ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: A thriller grows unbearably tense and steamy just before the last page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely tense' tempts you to take the outer letters of tense, but 'extremely' works alone; and 'before' gives letters rather than placing one piece ahead of another.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are defiant spoken phrases closing an argument, insisting nothing more is to be said on the matter.

clue.text: Policeman to pen in protesters getting something for tea?

blocks.note: copper is British slang for a police officer
kettling is the police tactic of confining demonstrators in a cordon

explanation.surface: A police officer contains a crowd of demonstrators and then gets something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: To kettle is a British police term for trapping protesters inside a cordon; the question mark marks the definition as describing an object, not a food.
explanation.definitionFit: A copper vessel for boiling water is used to brew a pot of the hot drink, so it is equipment needed for it.

clue.text: Yield is small hard fruit, we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters

blocks.note: a seed is a small hard fruit or kernel

explanation.surface: A gardener is told that the crop amounts to only small hard berries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yield' looks like a harvest in this garden picture, but it is the verb meaning give way.
explanation.definitionFit: To cede is to give up territory or concede a point, surrendering it to another party.

clue.text: After second month in France, you will be served up mildly obscene material

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means lifted, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
M is the abbreviation for month
tu is French for you

explanation.surface: A visitor arriving in France in February is offered rather saucy reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second month' looks like February, but it is two separate abbreviations, S and M.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut is indecent or suggestive talk, pictures or writing, crude rather than seriously pornographic.

clue.text: Two-thirds of wives-to-be selected 15th March, perhaps

indicators.note: taking two-thirds leaves out a third, so part of the word is dropped

blocks.note: brides are women about to be married

explanation.surface: Most of a group of brides chose the middle of March for their weddings.
explanation.walkthrough: Six letters lose their first two to leave four; 'perhaps' is there because in some months the day falls on the 13th.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the day in mid-month was so named; in March it fell on the 15th, when Caesar was killed.

clue.text: Fail to impress when lured astray before Mass

indicators.note: something gone astray has wandered off course, out of its proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the scientific abbreviation for mass

explanation.surface: A churchgoer tempted off course before the service turns out to be a disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' looks like the church service, but it is the physics quantity, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave people unmoved or disappointed is the opposite of overwhelming them, a jokey modern coinage.

clue.text: Remove some fibrous tissue

indicators.note: some means part of, so the letters are a portion of the words that follow

blocks.note: the answer runs across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A surgeon cuts away a piece of stringy tissue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remove' fits the surgical picture, but the answer straddles the two words that follow 'some'.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone is to force them out of a position, expelling or ejecting them.

clue.text: Doting, tender name?

indicators.note: doting can mean feeble-minded or muddled, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fond lover's pet name for their partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines and builds: 'doting' reads as fond, but in its older sense of muddled it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Terms such as darling or sweetheart are affectionate words of fondness used by lovers to each other.
